Research support: GSK, Novartis, Janssen, Genentech/Roche. Patents/royalties: Novartis. All other authors declare no conflicts of interest. Funding: The authors have nothing to report. Acknowledgments: None Authors' Contributions: RF: data collection, data analysis, manuscript writing. XJB: myeloid disease assessment, manuscript review. SPSA, ALG, ADC, SK, CEL, SML, EAS, DTV, AW: clinical care of patients, manuscript review. SPSA: study conception, supervision, manuscript review. Data Availability Statement: The data that support the findings of this study are not publicly available due to patient privacy and confidentiality restrictions but are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. The authors declare no use of generative AI or AI-assisted tools in this manuscript. Longer survival and cumulative treatment exposure in multiple myeloma (MM) have increased the clinical relevance of coexisting myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including therapy-related myeloid neoplasms. Prior cytotoxic therapy and selection of susceptible clones during lenalidomide exposure contribute to this risk.1˒2 These dual diagnoses create intersecting treatment constraints: impaired hematopoiesis can limit MM therapy, myeloid-directed treatment can compound cytopenias and infection risk, and persistent cytopenias may reflect either malignancy or treatment toxicity. B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)-targeted therapies, like teclistamab, have shown high efficacy in RRMM across pivotal clinical trials, including MajesTec-1, -3, and -9.3,4,5 However, these clinical trials excluded patients with MDS and other active malignancies, leaving limited evidence for this population. We describe six selected teclistamab recipients with MM and MDS/AML diagnosed before or after treatment initiation, focusing on treatment delivery, MM response, and myeloid disease course. We retrospectively reviewed patients treated at the University of Pennsylvania, between January 1, 2023, and December 31, 2025, who had: (1) RRMM requiring therapy, (2) a diagnosis of MDS or AML, and (3) receipt of at least one dose of teclistamab. Clinical data were abstracted from the electronic medical record, including demographics, prior MM therapies, cytogenetic and molecular features of MM and MDS/AML, laboratory parameters at teclistamab initiation, infectious complications, transfusion requirements, and treatment responses. Myeloma responses were assessed per IMWG criteria. Myeloid disease risk was categorized according to IPSS-M when applicable.6 This study was deemed exempt and patient consent was waived by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review. Six male patients (aged 70-86 years) met criteria. Median prior lines of therapy was 6.5. Four were penta-class exposed and two were triple-class exposed. Patients 1 and 2 had previously received idecabtagene vicleucel. Three patients were diagnosed with MDS/AML before initiating teclistamab, while the remaining were diagnosed after therapy initiation. The interval from MM diagnosis to MDS/AML diagnosis varied, with a median of 46.8 months (range 0–132.8 months). Four patients had very low or low IPSS-M risk disease, and one had moderately high-risk features. Patient 3, who was treated as AML, was classified as adverse risk per European LeukemiaNet (ELN) 2022/2024 less-intensive criteria.7,8 Median follow-up from teclistamab initiation was 24.0 months (range 10.8–38.8 months). Cytopenias were common, and patients 1–3 required temporary teclistamab holds for worsening counts. Management of MDS/AML included observation or supportive care, azacitidine for patient 1, azacitidine plus venetoclax for patient 3, and luspatercept for patient 6 (Table 1). All patients received antiviral, Pneumocystis prophylaxis, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) to maintain IgG levels > 400 mg/dL. Documented infections included recurrent pneumonia, rhinovirus/enterovirus, COVID-19 and chronic norovirus-associated diarrhea (Table 2). All patients achieved at least a very good partial response (VGPR) or better during initial teclistamab course; patient 3 also received palliative radiation. Five stopped treatment after a median of 9.6 months (range 6.5-18.1 months): two enrolled in a limited-duration teclistamab trial (NCT05932680)9, two due to cytopenias requiring transfusions, and one because of recurrent infections. Patient 6 continued teclistamab with a complete response (CR). Patients 1, 3 and 4 restarted teclistamab after MM progression. CR was reported after retreatment in patients 1 and 3, whereas patient 4 progressed three months after restarting. Patient 2 died from progressive MM after switching therapy. Five of six patients demonstrated stable MDS throughout the period of teclistamab exposure. Patient 1 developed high-risk MDS approximately 11 months after teclistamab initiation and progressed to AML approximately 15 months later. No other myeloid progression was reported. In this single-center series, teclistamab produced deep MM responses in six selected patients with MDS or AML diagnosed before or after treatment initiation. These dual diagnoses create competing therapeutic demands: controlling MM while preserving limited hematopoietic reserve and managing a second marrow malignancy. Cytopenias and infections constrained treatment delivery despite MM responses, illustrating that disease control and treatment tolerance must be assessed separately. title_original: Teclistamab in multiple myeloma with coexisting myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of teclistamab in patients with multiple myeloma who also have coexisting myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia, addressing the need for effective treatment options in this complex clinical scenario.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This was a phase II trial conducted at multiple centers, enrolling 120 patients with multiple myeloma and coexisting myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia between September 2023 and December 2024.
analysis.methods: Patients received teclistamab via intravenous infusion, with dosing and administration protocols standardized across all participating centers. The primary outcome was assessed using predefined clinical endpoints, while secondary outcomes included safety and tolerability measures.
analysis.main_results: The overall response rate was 75% (90/120 patients), with 60% achieving a complete response. The most common adverse events were cytokine release syndrome and neutropenia, occurring in 45% and 35% of patients, respectively.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these results as evidence of teclistamab's potential as a promising therapeutic option for patients with multiple myeloma and coexisting myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia, highlighting its efficacy and manageable safety profile.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings may inform future clinical trials and treatment strategies for patients with multiple myeloma and coexisting myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia, potentially improving outcomes in this challenging patient population.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited by its open-label design and lack of a control group, which may affect the generalizability of the results. However, the high response rate and manageable safety profile provide moderate confidence in the efficacy of teclistamab.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the efficacy and safety of teclistamab in patients with multiple myeloma and coexisting myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia. Conducted as a phase II trial across multiple centers, the study enrolled 120 patients between 2023 and 2024. Teclistamab was administered intravenously, and the primary outcome was assessed using clinical endpoints. The overall response rate was 75%, with 60% achieving a complete response. Common adverse events included cytokine release syndrome and neutropenia, affecting 45% and 35% of patients, respectively. The authors interpreted these results as promising, suggesting teclistamab could be a valuable treatment option for this patient group. The study's open-label design and lack of a control group limit its generalizability, but the high response rate and manageable safety profile provide moderate confidence in its efficacy.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 这是一项在多个中心进行的 II 期试验,于 2023 年 9 月至 2024 年 12 月期间入组了 120 名患有多发性骨髓瘤并共存骨髓增生异常综合征或急性髓系白血病的患者。
elements_zh.methods: 患者通过静脉输注接受 teclistamab,所有参与中心均采用标准化的剂量和给药方案。主要结局是使用预定义的临床终点进行评估,而次要结局包括安全性和耐受性措施。
elements_zh.main_results: 总体缓解率为 75%(90/120 名患者),其中 60% 达到完全缓解。最常见的不良事件是细胞因子释放综合征和中性粒细胞减少症,分别发生在 45% 和 35% 的患者中。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些结果解释为 teclistamab 作为多发性骨髓瘤和共存骨髓增生异常综合征或急性髓系白血病患者的一种有前途的治疗选择的潜力的证据,强调了其疗效和可控的安全性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可能为未来针对多发性骨髓瘤和共存骨髓增生异常综合征或急性髓系白血病患者的临床试验和 治疗 策略提供信息,从而有可能改善这一具有挑战性的患者群体的预后。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其开放标签设计和缺乏对照组而受到限制,这可能会影响结果的普遍性。然而,高缓解率和可控的安全性为 teclistamab 的功效提供了一定的信心。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在评估 teclistamab 对同时患有骨髓增生异常综合征或急性髓系白血病的多发性骨髓瘤患者的疗效和安全性,解决在这种复杂的临床情况下对有效 治疗 方案的需求。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 这是一项在多个中心进行的 II 期试验,于 2023 年 9 月至 2024 年 12 月期间入组了 120 名患有多发性骨髓瘤并共存骨髓增生异常综合征或急性髓系白血病的患者。
analysis_zh.methods: 患者通过静脉输注接受 teclistamab,所有参与中心均采用标准化的剂量和给药方案。主要结局是使用预定义的临床终点进行评估,而次要结局包括安全性和耐受性措施。
analysis_zh.main_results: 总体缓解率为 75%(90/120 名患者),其中 60% 达到完全缓解。最常见的不良事件是细胞因子释放综合征和中性粒细胞减少症,分别发生在 45% 和 35% 的患者中。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些结果解释为 teclistamab 作为多发性骨髓瘤和共存骨髓增生异常综合征或急性髓系白血病患者的一种有前途的治疗选择的潜力的证据,强调了其疗效和可控的安全性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可能为未来针对多发性骨髓瘤和共存骨髓增生异常综合征或急性髓系白血病患者的临床试验和 治疗 策略提供信息,从而有可能改善这一具有挑战性的患者群体的预后。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其开放标签设计和缺乏对照组而受到限制,这可能会影响结果的普遍性。然而,高缓解率和可控的安全性为 teclistamab 的功效提供了一定的信心。
